nh_humphrey_s_ledge.blurb: A small winter cliff a short drive beyond Cathedral Ledge in the North Conway valley, useful when the bigger walls are crowded. Nearly all of its 18 climbs are water ice, running from easy WI2 up to WI4, with most sitting at WI3 and a handful at WI4. One mixed line at the easy end rounds out the list. It sits low in the valley, with a modest elevation of a few hundred feet above sea level, so it suits climbers looking for moderate ice in a quieter setting than the main ledges.

nh_diedre_area_the.blurb: A section of Cathedral Ledge above North Conway, given over almost entirely to traditional climbing on granite. The eighteen routes follow corners and cracks of every width, from fingers to off-width, and the exposure is considerable. Grades start around 5.9 and climb steadily: a few 5.10s, a large block of 5.11s, several 5.12s and one 5.13 test piece. This is not a place for beginners. The rock quality is praised throughout and the long crack lines are well protected. Bring a full rack and be comfortable on sustained crack climbing.

nh_welch_mountain.blurb: Welch Mountain, in the Waterville Valley area, offers a scatter of small granite crags near the summit, reached on the hiking loop that also serves its neighbour Dickey. Expect short but good trad routes, mostly easy to moderate with a single 5.11, plus a top-rope line and about nine boulder problems from the very easiest up to V7. The views from the cliffs are a big part of the appeal. Carry a small rack and a rope for the roped lines; the hike in is long enough that this suits a day out combining a walk and a few climbs.

nh_high_camp_cliff.blurb: A high-elevation cliff on the southeast side of Mt Osceola, at roughly 3,900 feet, within the High Camp Crags group. Its 18 routes are mostly bolted or mixed-protection lines in a modern style, with a good spread: a few in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, a cluster at 5.10, and more at 5.11 through 5.13. The altitude makes it a cooler summer choice than the valley walls, though afternoon thunderstorms can arrive fast. Bring a light rack and a 60 m rope, and allow for a long uphill hike before you reach the wall.
nh_high_camp_cliff.approach: Follow the Osceola trail from the road for about two miles, then leave it near a sharp left turn and take a faint path through the woods past a small campsite. The path firms up and reaches the wall in under ten minutes; a climbers' trail leads to the left side of the cliff.

nh_lower_slabs.blurb: Gentle granite slabs in Pawtuckaway State Park, popular with families, camps and newer climbers. Most of the 17 climbs are set up as top ropes, with trees for anchors and an easy walk to the top, and the rest are short trad lines. Grades are friendly: lots of 5.4 to 5.8, with a few steps up to 5.10 and two 5.11 lines. The cliff sits beside a swampy pond, so mosquitoes can be fierce in summer. It can be busy on fine days, and the nearby upper cliff is the fallback if the slabs are occupied.
nh_lower_slabs.parking_note: Use the horse farm parking area off the park road; if that is full, additional pull-outs and the pond-side parking are alternatives.
nh_lower_slabs.approach: From the horse farm lot, follow the dirt trail for roughly ten minutes until large boulders appear on the right, then take the signed path just before the pond; the slabs lie below the upper cliffs.

nh_04_highlander_wall.blurb: The steepest stretch of the broken cliff band in Sandwich Notch, and the place where most of the notch's bolted routes live. Of its 17 climbs, eleven are sport and six are trad, so a standard rack is worth bringing for the crack lines. The grades lean towards the harder end: one easy route, then mostly 5.9 through 5.12 with a cluster of 5.10s and several 5.12s. It is a quiet setting beside a brook, a short walk off a dirt road, and well suited to climbers who want steep, sustained pitches rather than beginner terrain.
nh_04_highlander_wall.parking_note: Drive Sandwich Notch Road beyond Beede Falls and over the brook's two small bridges to the Pulpit Rock pull-off, where there is room for a handful of cars.
nh_04_highlander_wall.approach: Walk back down the road a short way, pick up a faint path, and cross the brook; it leads straight to the first climbs on the wall.

nh_roadhouse.blurb: A friendly little crag in the Russell Crags group near Woodstock and Lincoln, set low on the hill in the forest and easy to reach. It holds 17 climbs with a mix of styles: twelve sport routes, five trad and a top rope. The grades are approachable, with a good number around 5.7 and a spread up to the low 5.12 range. A fixed rope in the middle gives access to routes above the slab. It makes a pleasant stop for climbers wanting variety, from easy leads to a few harder bolted pitches.
nh_roadhouse.approach: Take the stream trail from the gate; the crag is the next one along after Forest Garden.
